_note: The Gym manifest (WP25a): which grammar points act as selectable form categories, grouped into picker columns. 'point' must match the grammar point title exactly (resolved to ids at request time). 'usage' is the plain-language hover explanation; 'example' is a real drill sentence from that point. 'nonstandard': entries hidden behind the 'include non-standard words' toggle.

entries.label: Copulas ni / jẹ́
entries.usage: Use these to say what or who somebody is: jẹ́ goes before the word (Mo jẹ́ olùkọ́), ni goes after it (Olùkọ́ ni mí).
entries.example: Mo jẹ́ olùkọ́. — I am a teacher.

entries.label: wà (be located)
entries.usage: Use wà to say where somebody or something is, with ní in front of the place.
entries.example: Bàbá wà ní oko. — Father is at the farm.

entries.label: Progressive ń
entries.usage: Put ń in front of the verb when the action is going on right now.
entries.example: Mo ń kàwé. — I am reading.

entries.label: Perfect ti
entries.usage: Put ti in front of the verb when the thing is already done — have eaten, have arrived.
entries.example: Mo ti jẹun. — I have (already) eaten.

entries.label: Future máa / yóò
entries.usage: Put máa (everyday speech) or yóò (fuller, more formal) before the verb for something that has not happened yet.
entries.example: Mo máa lọ ní ọ̀la. — I will go tomorrow.

entries.label: Habitual máa ń
entries.usage: Use máa ń for what somebody does again and again — every morning, every Saturday; kì í is the never-does version.
entries.example: Mo máa ń jí ní aago mẹ́fà. — I usually wake up at six o'clock.

entries.label: Adjective verbs
entries.usage: Describing words like dára (be good) and tóbi (be big) act as the verb themselves — never add a word for is.
entries.example: Oúnjẹ yìí dára. — This food is good.

entries.label: Commands & má
entries.usage: Use the plain verb on its own to tell somebody to do something, and put má in front of it to tell them not to.
entries.example: Wá síbí! — Come here!

entries.point: Modals fẹ́, lè, gbọ́dọ̀ (want / can / must)
entries.label: Modals fẹ́ / lè
entries.usage: Slot fẹ́ (want), lè (can) or gbọ́dọ̀ (must) between the person and the verb.
entries.example: Mo fẹ́ jẹun báyìí. — I want to eat now.

entries.label: Láti (to do)
entries.usage: Put láti before a verb to say why you did something, or after words like it is hard / it is easy.
entries.example: Mo wá láti kọ́ èdè Yorùbá. — I came to learn Yoruba.

entries.label: Subject pronouns
entries.usage: Use these short words right before the verb to say who is doing it: mo (I), o (you), ó (he/she), a (we), ẹ (you all), wọ́n (they).
entries.example: Mo fẹ́ omi. — I want water.

entries.label: Object pronouns
entries.usage: Use these after the verb for whoever is on the receiving end: mi, ẹ, i, wa, yín, wọn.
entries.example: Mo rí i ní ọjà. — I saw him/her at the market.

entries.label: Tone pairs
entries.usage: Use this when two words look alike apart from their marks — ọkọ́ (hoe), ọkọ (husband), ọkọ̀ (vehicle) — and you have to pick the one the sentence means.
entries.example: Mo ní ọkọ̀ kan. — I have a vehicle.

entries.label: Plural àwọn
entries.usage: Put àwọn in front of a noun when it matters that there is more than one; leave it out when a number is already there.
entries.example: Àwọn ọmọ ń ṣeré. — The children are playing.

entries.label: Possessives
entries.usage: Put mi, rẹ, rẹ̀, wa or wọn after the noun to say whose it is: ìwé mi is my book.
entries.example: Ìwé mi wà níbí. — My book is here.

entries.label: This / that
entries.usage: Put yìí (this) or yẹn (that) after the noun to point out which one you mean; náà means the one already spoken about.
entries.example: Ìwé yìí dára. — This book is good.

entries.point: Numbers after the noun (ìwé méjì, mélòó)
entries.label: Numbers after nouns
entries.usage: Put the number after the thing you are counting, and put mélòó in the same place to ask how many.
entries.example: Mo ra ìwé méjì. — I bought two books.

entries.label: Noun prefixes
entries.usage: Build a word for a person or a thing: olù- for the one who does it, oní-/alá- for the one who owns or sells it, ì- for the activity itself.
entries.example: Olùkọ́ wa kọ́ wa ní èdè Gẹ̀ẹ́sì. — Our teacher teaches us English.

entries.label: Reduplication
entries.usage: Double the front of a verb to talk about the activity itself (jẹ eat becomes jíjẹ eating), and double a whole word to strengthen it (kíákíá quickly).
entries.example: Jíjẹ oúnjẹ tó dára ṣe pàtàkì. — Eating good food is important.

entries.label: Respectful ẹ / ẹ̀yin
entries.usage: Say ẹ or ẹ̀yin instead of o when speaking to one older or senior person — greetings and thanks nearly always use it.
entries.example: 'Ẹ káàárọ̀, mà!' ọmọ náà kí ìyá àgbà. — 'Good morning, ma!' the child greeted the old woman.

entries.label: Negation kò
entries.usage: Put kò in front of the verb to say something is not so; for there is no…, use kò sí.
entries.example: Ó kò fẹ́ oúnjẹ. — He does not want food.

entries.point: Questions with ṣé and kí ni
entries.label: Ṣé & kí ni
entries.usage: Start a statement with ṣé to turn it into a yes-or-no question, or with kí ni to ask what something is.
entries.example: Ṣé o fẹ́ omi? — Do you want water?

entries.point: Question words (ta ni, níbo, báwo, èló)
entries.label: Who / where / how
entries.usage: Open with ta ni (who), níbo (where), báwo (how), èló (how much) or nígbà wo (when), and carry on with ni.
entries.example: Ta ni ó kọ ìwé yìí? — Who wrote this book?

entries.label: Focus with ni
entries.usage: Move the part you want to stress to the front and add ni after it — it was ADÉ who went, it was the MARKET I went to.
entries.example: Adé ni ó lọ. — It was Adé who went.

entries.label: Relative tí
entries.usage: Use tí to hang a whole description on a noun: the man WHO came, the book THAT I bought.
entries.example: Ọkùnrin tí ó wá jẹ́ olùkọ́. — The man who came is a teacher.

entries.label: Serial verbs
entries.usage: String verbs one after another with no word for and when a single action runs through them: mú ìwé wá, take-book-come, means bring the book.
entries.example: Mú ìwé wá fún mi. — Bring me the book (take-book-come).

entries.point: Serial verbs with fi and fún
entries.label: fi / fún serials
entries.usage: Add fi to name the tool used (fi ọ̀bẹ gé, cut it with a knife) and fún to name who it is for (ra fún mi, buy it for me).
entries.example: Ó fi ọ̀bẹ gé ẹran. — He cut the meat with a knife.

entries.label: If: bí … bá
entries.usage: Use bí at the start and bá just before the verb for something that may still happen.
entries.example: Bí o bá kàwé, wàá yege. — If you study, you will pass.

entries.label: Comparison ju … lọ
entries.usage: Wrap ju … lọ around whatever you are measuring against; the describing word itself stays as it is.
entries.example: Ó ga ju mí lọ. — He is taller than me.

entries.label: Reported pé
entries.usage: Use pé after say, know, hear or think to report what somebody said; inside the report, òun points back at the speaker.
entries.example: Ó sọ pé òun máa wá. — He said that he would come.

entries.point: Kí clauses — wishes and indirect commands
entries.label: Kí clauses
entries.usage: Use kí for what somebody should do or what you hope happens — I want you to come, may your day be good.
entries.example: Mo fẹ́ kí o wá ní àárọ̀. — I want you to come in the morning.

entries.label: Impersonal wọ́n
entries.usage: Say wọ́n (they), meaning nobody in particular, where English would say something was done to something — the house was sold, you are being called.
entries.example: Wọ́n ti kọ́ ilé náà. — The house has been built (lit. they have built it).

entries.point: Although: bí ó tilẹ̀ jẹ́ pé
entries.label: Even though
entries.usage: Open with bí ó tilẹ̀ jẹ́ pé when the second half happens in spite of the first; síbẹ̀ (nevertheless) does the same job between two sentences.
entries.example: Bí ó tilẹ̀ jẹ́ pé òjò rọ̀, a lọ. — Even though it rained, we went.

entries.point: Ní vs sí — at a place vs towards it
entries.label: Ní vs sí
entries.usage: Use ní when nothing moves (wà ní ilé, is at home) and sí when something goes somewhere (lọ sí ọjà, went to the market).
entries.example: Bàbá wà ní oko. — Father is at the farm.

entries.point: Time clauses: nígbà tí, lẹ́yìn tí, kí … tó
entries.label: Time clauses
entries.usage: Say how two events line up in time: nígbà tí (when), lẹ́yìn tí (after), kí … tó (before).
entries.example: Nígbà tí mo dé, òjò ń rọ̀. — When I arrived, it was raining.

entries.label: Chaining with sì
entries.usage: Join two things the same person did one after the other, putting sì just after the doer in the second part.
entries.example: Ó dé ilé, ó sì jókòó. — He arrived home and sat down.

entries.label: How: bí … ṣe
entries.usage: Use bí … ṣe to talk about the way something is done — how I saw it, how the machine works.
entries.example: Èyí ni bí mo ṣe rí i. — This is how I saw it.

entries.label: Intensifiers
entries.usage: Each describing word has its own partner word for very — funfun láúláú (spotlessly white), gbóná janjan (piping hot) — and the pairs cannot be swapped.
entries.example: Aṣọ náà funfun láúláú. — The cloth is spotlessly white.

entries.point: Òwe — proverbs, the horses of speech
entries.label: Proverbs (òwe)
entries.usage: Drop in a proverb, word for word, when you want to settle a point or carry an argument home.
entries.example: Òwe ni ẹṣin ọ̀rọ̀. — Proverbs are the horses of speech.

entries.label: Discourse particles
entries.usage: Add these small words to colour what you say: o (warmth or urgency), ná (for now), ṣebí (surely…?), gan-an (really), tilẹ̀ (even).
entries.example: Ó dàbọ̀ o! — Goodbye o! (warm)
